Issued at 518 AM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

Confidence is high that a robust troughing pattern will be in place 
over the Eastern CONUS at the beginning of the long term forecast 
period. The model guidance suite collectively resolves the parent 
longwave feature digging deeper into the Ohio River Valley between 
Thursday night and Saturday morning, with a series of embedded 
shortwave disturbances rotating through the forecast area as it does 
so. These impulses will keep Eastern Kentucky's weather active in 
this time frame, as the related precipitation chances will overlap 
with a persistent cold air advection regime and upsloped low-level 
winds. This combination should yield the first snowflakes of the 
season on Friday, but widespread, meaningful winter weather impacts 
are not anticipated. Rather, this system will act as an appetizer 
for the upcoming winter weather season, with sensible weather 
impacts largely limited to noticeably colder temperatures for the 
rest of the forecast period. 

When the period opens on Thursday night, rain showers will likely be 
ongoing across the forecast area. Northwesterly surface flow in the 
wake of the previous day's frontal passage will allow temperatures 
to cool into the mid 30s overnight, but the attendant cloud coverage 
will inhibit radiational cooling and mute the diurnal cooling curve. 
So, the baseline deterministic NBM low temperature guidance appears 
too cold, despite the near-surface CAA. This event recently entered 
the temporal range of higher-resolution ensemble guidance, which 
confines >20% probabilities for freezing temperatures on Friday 
morning to the mountains along the Virginia state line. Minimum and 
hourly temperature grids were blended towards CONS guidance to 
account for this, but the colder temperatures were retained at the 
mountaintops. The freezing probabilities atop Big Black Mountain are 
actually above 75%, which suggests that those higher terrain locales 
will be the first to experience a changeover to wintery 
precipitation. Expect a cool rain to dominate elsewhere at first, 
although colder air is expected to move in aloft on Friday morning. 

As the additional shortwave disturbances rotate around the base of 
the digging parent trough on Friday, they will provide sufficient 
dynamic lift for continued precipitation chances across the Ohio 
River Valley. The passage of each disturbance will be marked by 
shifts towards northwesterly flow aloft and thus a deeper cold air 
advection regime. Modeled critical thickness values drop below the 
540 decameter threshold area-wide by dawn, when model soundings 
depict subfreezing temperatures at 950mb and above. The lack of a 
warm nose/melting layer in those soundings effectively (and 
thankfully) rules out any sleet and freezing rain potential in this 
setup, but the growing influence of the cold aloft should allow snow 
to mix with the rain outside of the mountain locales on Friday 
morning. The longevity of those snow chances is uncertain, as 
filtered diurnal heating should keep surface temperatures above-
freezing through the daytime hours. Rain should remain the dominant 
precipitation type through the afternoon hours, but temperatures 
will struggle to warm much higher than the low/mid 40s amidst the 
deepening CAA regime. These below-normal highs will set the stage 
for temperatures to easily drop below freezing-area wide on Friday 
night, when a full changeover to snow is possible in the higher 
terrain locales of Southeast Kentucky. The greatest and longest-
duration PoPs on Friday and Friday night will come in places with 
northwest-facing slopes. There, orographic lift will combine with 
the aforementioned dynamic components and a fetch of moisture off 
Lake Michigan to squeeze out the most precipitation. Accumulation 
potential is limited by the lack of an antecedent cold spell, but a 
dusting/trace cannot be ruled out in places along and east of the 
Pottsville Escarpment. The LREF resolves a >20% chance of at least 
0.01 inches of snow in the SE half of the JKL CWA through Saturday 
morning, with the greatest chances for measurable snow atop Pine and 
Black Mountains. There, those probabilities jump to between 50 and 
70%. If the accumulation threshold is raised to an inch, chances 
drop to less than 25%, with contours confined entirely to the tops 
of the Mountains. 

The current storm total snow grids mirror these accumulation 
probabilities, with only a few tenths forecast in the higher-terrain 
locales of Bell, Harlan, Letcher, and Pike Counties. A dusting 
cannot be ruled out further to the northwest, and neither can an 
over-performance atop Black Mountain. Pattern recognition and past 
experience suggest that cloud coverage and upslope PoPs will be
